How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

As video games have grown from a niche pastime into a major cultural medium, they have reached broader audiences and transformed the social context of play, whether alone or with others. We ask whether the motivations engaged by the games themselves have changed over time. In Study 1, we used a large language model, validated against human coding, to annotate 11,359 commercially released games from 1993 to 2016 on 48 motivational ingredients, including status-seeking, revenge, affiliation, compassion, and curiosity. We normalized within each game to represent its relative motivational composition. Over this period, the average competitive index (the share of a game's motivational content devoted to competition, dominance, and aggression) fell from 41% to 26%, while the prosocial index (affiliation, warmth, and care) rose from 11% to 24%. This reallocation held within genres and franchises, in both single-and multiplayer titles, and under all 642,560 admissible definitions of the two indices. In Study 2, 4,498 players reported their favorite games and completed a Big Five measure. Higher Agreeableness predicted a balance favoring prosocial over agonistic content, driven primarily by lower agonistic content, whereas higher Extraversion, particularly Sociability, predicted a balance favoring agonistic content. This contrast suggests that a disposition towards social engagement is distinct from a preference for caring social content. Together, the studies document a "prosocial turn" in the motivational content of video games: a historical reallocation from competition and dominance towards affiliation, warmth, and care. The direction of this shift aligns with contemporary personality differences in content preference.

1. Introduction

For many players, playing video games is a deeply social activity. Contemporary games increasingly support interaction with other players (Granic et al., 2014), and online worlds can foster lasting friendships, social capital, and a sense of belonging (Cole & Griffiths, 2007; Domahidi et al., 2014; Trepte et al., 2012; Ferguson & Olson, 2013; Raith et al., 2021). Players also commonly identify social connection as a reason for playing online games (Yee, 2006; Yee et al., 2012). Although greater involvement in online gaming has sometimes been associated with lower perceived social support, the direction of this relationship remains unclear (Kowert et al., 2014). Taken together, this literature portrays gaming not simply as a solitary pastime but as a social context in which people meet, cooperate, form relationships, and develop a sense of belonging.

Much of this work, however, concerns the social context of play -with whom players play, communicate, and form relationships -rather than the motivational content of games themselves: what games are about and which motivations they engage. As video games developed from a niche pastime into a global medium, networked technologies transformed this context by creating new opportunities for players to interact through games. Yet changes in how games are played need not imply corresponding changes in what games are about. These two dimensions are distinct and can vary independently: a competitive shooter played with friends is social in context but agonistic in content; conversely, a single-player game centered on tending a village and caring for its inhabitants is solitary in context but prosocial in content. The transformation of gaming's social context therefore raises a parallel historical question about the games themselves: did the motivations they engage change as well? To our knowledge, no study has examined this question at sufficient scale and over a sufficiently long period to determine whether, and in what direction, such a shift occurred.

Such a change could matter for at least two reasons. First, the content of a popular medium may offer a window onto the preferences of its audience. Cultural artefacts partly reflect the psychological traits and concerns of the people who produce and consume them and can therefore serve as "cognitive fossils" of past preferences and motivations (Baumard et al., 2024). Their content has been used to trace historical changes ranging from the increasing prominence of cooperation in early modern fiction (Martins & Baumard, 2020) to changing displays of trustworthiness across six centuries of European portraiture (Safra et al., 2020). A historical shift in the motivational content of video games could similarly provide indirect evidence about the preferences to which the medium catered over time. By the same logic, differences among contemporary players should be reflected in the motivational content of the games they prefer.

Second, game content may influence players' attitudes and behavior beyond play. Previous research suggests that the social framing of this content may matter: games organized around helping and cooperation have been linked to greater helping and empathy (Gentile et al., 2009; Greitemeyer & Osswald, 2010; Prot et al., 2014), whereas content centered on harm and interpersonal conflict has sometimes been associated with more aggressive responding and less prosocial behavior (Anderson et al., 2010). Although the magnitude and robustness of these effects remain debated (see Ferguson, 2015, for a critical assessment), even modest effects could matter when exposure is sustained and widespread.

We address these questions in two complementary studies. Study 1 tracks historical changes in the motivational content of 11,359 commercially released games between 1993 and 2016. Study 2 turns from historical change at the level of the medium to variation among contemporary players, asking, in an independent sample of 4,498 players, whether personality predicts the motivational content of the games they name as favorites. Together, the studies examine both whether the motivational content of games has changed and whether the direction of that change aligns with personality-related differences in players' content preferences.

2. Study 1: The motivational content of games shifted from competitive to prosocial

>Study 1: The motivational content of games shifted from competitive to prosocial >Method

2.1.1 Data

We drew on the VGChartz catalog, which records commercially released video games together with their release year, genre, platform, and regional and global sales. Because a title released on multiple platforms appears once for each platform, we aggregated these platform-specific entries into a single game release, defined as a unique title-year combination. For each release, we retained a single content annotation, averaging the ingredient scores across platform entries when these differed (6.6% of the resulting scores are therefore non-integer). We summed sales across platforms and retained the number of platforms as a covariate. Remakes and reissues sharing a title but released in different years were treated as distinct releases. To ensure adequate annual coverage, we restricted the analysis to years containing at least 30 titles, yielding a contiguous period from 1993 to 2016. The final corpus comprised 11,359 game releases with complete content annotations and associated metadata.

2.1.2 Motivational Ingredient Framework

To characterize the motivational content of games, we drew on a framework that represents cultural products as combinations of the evolved human motivations they engage (Dubourg, Thouzeau, et al., 2026). The framework builds on the fundamental-motives tradition in cognitive science, according to which human motivation comprises a set of distinct systems shaped to address recurrent adaptive problems (Kenrick et al., 2010). These include acquiring food and water, avoiding predators and pathogens, gaining status, forming and defending coalitions, attracting and retaining mates, and caring for kin (Kenrick et al., 2010; Schaller et al., 2017; Neel et al., 2016). Each system is proposed to have its own eliciting conditions and associated rewards and to operate with some degree of independence from the others.

From this perspective, cultural products owe part of their appeal to their capacity to engage these motivational systems (Dubourg, Thouzeau, et al., 2026; Dubourg & Baumard, 2022). A work can therefore be characterized not only by its genre but also by the particular set of motivations it engages -its motivational "recipe". The framework distinguishes 48 such ingredients, spanning basic drives (e.g., hunger, thirst, Sleepiness), epistemic motivations (e.g., curiosity, explanation-seeking), and social, moral, and status-related concerns (e.g., affiliation, warmth, compassion, status-seeking, revenge, moral blame). Works within the same genre may have different motivational recipes, whereas works from different genres may share many of the same ingredients.

Video games are particularly well-suited to this framework because they can be described in terms of the opportunities they offer players to pursue or fulfill different motivations (Dubourg & Chambon, 2025). A survival game such as Don't Starve, for example, engages motivations related to hunger, thirst, and fear of predators; a farming-and-village simulation such as Stardew Valley engages affiliation, friendship, warmth, and parental care; a competitive shooter such as Call of Duty engages status-seeking, coalitional affiliation, and aggression. Individual ingredients can therefore recur across otherwise very different games: curiosity, for example, may be engaged by both a puzzle game and an open-world adventure. Conversely, a single game may combine numerous ingredients, as when a role-playing game engages curiosity, friendship, moral choice, and status simultaneously. This common motivational vocabulary allows games to be compared across genres and provides a basis for examining whether the relative prevalence of these ingredients has changed over time.

2.1.3 Annotation

We annotated games using a large language model. Recent studies suggest that, for some annotation and classification tasks, large language models can achieve performance comparable to or better than that of trained human coders, often at substantially lower cost and with greater consistency (Gilardi et al., 2023; Rathje et al., 2024; see also : Pei et al., 2023; Bongini et al., 2023). This LLM-based approach has also been used and validated in previous applications of the motivational-ingredient taxonomy (Dubourg et al., 2024; Dubourg, Thouzeau, et al., 2026; Dubourg & Thouzeau, 2026).

Each game was rated on all 48 ingredients using OpenAI's GPT-5.4. The model was prompted to act as an expert in psychology and video game analysis and to treat the experience of the human player -not that of the in-game character -as the unit of analysis. For each ingredient, it rated both its presence and its importance to the player's experience on an anchored scale ranging from 0 to 6. Selected anchors included0 = Absent, indicating that the game offered no opportunity to fulfill the motivation;3 = Supported, indicating that occasional moments or mechanics allowed the player to fulfill it;4 = Emphasized, indicating that fulfilling the motivation was integral to the experience; and6 = Defining, indicating that removing it would fundamentally alter the meaning of the game. Scores were restricted to motivations directly engaged through the player's own perceptual, affective, or bodily experience, regardless of whether the player consciously pursues them. For each ingredient, the model generated a one-to two-sentence justification before assigning its score.

Each game was annotated in a single call covering all 48 ingredients, with the definition of each ingredient included in the prompt. The model returned a structured JSON object containing a justification and a score for each ingredient. If the model lacked sufficient confidence to score a particular ingredient for a title, that value was recorded as missing. All annotations were processed through the OpenAI Batch API. Missing scores were extremely rare: 41 of the 545,232 ingredient scores in the final corpus (0.008%) were missing, affecting 18 of the 11,359 releases.

2.1.4 Validation

Temporal trends derived from LLM annotations can fail in two ways. The first is a false negative: undirected scoring noise (e.g., hallucination) may attenuate the association with release year, causing a genuine trend to be missed. Although increasing the size of the corpus does not eliminate this measurement error, it reduces the minimum annotation quality required to detect the effect. The second is a false positive: annotation errors that vary systematically with release year may produce a spurious temporal trend. Increasing the corpus size does not reduce such bias. Instead, it narrows the confidence interval around the biased estimate, potentially making even a small systematic error appear conclusive (Meng, 2018).

To evaluate these two risks, we followed the design-specific validation procedure developed by Dubourg and Thouzeau (2026). Rather than applying a generic agreement threshold, this procedure derives the level of annotation quality and systematic bias that the specific design can tolerate. One author independently hand-coded 99 games released between 1994 and 2016 on all 21 ingredients composing the two indices (12 prosocial, 9 competitive), using the same 0-6 scale and definitions provided to the model. The coder did not have access to the model's scores. Because the relevant validation thresholds depend on the effect size and sample size obtained in the study, we report the complete validation analysis after presenting the main results. In addition, we used the audit to correct the corpus-level estimate for annotation error using prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023).

2.1.5 Analyses

We represented each game as a relative composition rather than as a set of absolute motivational scores. This choice was motivated by a general increase in motivational richness over time: the mean summed across all 48 ingredients rose from 54.3 in 1993 to 78.6 in 2016, corresponding to an estimated increase of 10.1 points per decade (p < .001). As a result, increases in the raw scores of individual ingredients may reflect a general expansion of motivational scope rather than a specific shift towards those ingredients. For illustration, Tetris 2 (1993) received a summed score of 37, whereas The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (2015) received a score of 159. Tetris 2 is an abstract puzzle game that engages relatively few motivational systems beyond skill and mastery. By contrast, The Witcher 3 is an open-world RPG whose narrative and mechanics engage a broad range of motivations, including romance, kinship, moral choice, status, fear, and revenge. This contrast illustrates the broader expansion of motivational scope associated with more narratively complex and systems-rich game design.

An increase in the absolute prosocial score would therefore be ambiguous: it could reflect either a specific increase in prosocial content or the general expansion of motivational richness observed across games. To distinguish between these possibilities, we normalized the 48 scores for each game so that they summed to one: where x ij is the raw score of game i on ingredient j, and s ij is the corresponding share of that game's total motivational content.

Because these shares sum to one, an increase in the share of one ingredient must be offset by a decrease in the combined share of others. The resulting measure therefore captures changes in the relative composition of motivational content rather than changes in its overall level.

For the central analysis, we grouped a subset of the 48 ingredients into two functional indices defined on theoretical grounds. Ingredients were classified not according to their affective valence but according to their primary social function. The prosocial index (P) summed the normalized shares of 12 ingredients associated with cooperation, attachment, and moral care: Warmth, Moral praise, Compassion, Affiliation, Friendship, Parental protection, Parental investment, Familial love, Moral pride, Guilt, Forgiveness, and Moral blame. The competitive index (C) summed the normalized shares of 9 ingredients associated with rank, dominance, and conflict: Fear of aggressors, Revenge, Status-seeking, Envy, Hatred, Coalitional affiliation, Anger, Pride, and Shame. The remaining 27 ingredients (e.g., Hunger, Curiosity, Skill acquisition) were assigned to neither pole and were analyzed individually. Both indices are computed per game and averaged across the games released each year, rather than pooled within years, which would implicitly weight years by motivational richness (r = .58 with the prosocial index).

Because our primary aim was to estimate historical change, the main analyses were conducted at the level of release year. Each index is reported on two scales: as a share of the game's summed 48-ingredient content, and as the mean per ingredient (dividing by 12 and 9), which places the two poles on a common scale. For each index taken separately, these are the same quantity expressed differently. We regressed the annual mean of each index on release year and scaled year so that the coefficients represent percentage-point changes per decade. To summarize the relative balance between the two poles in a single quantity, we also computed the prosocial share, Q, from the per-ingredient values of P and C: Q = P / (P + C) Unlike P and C taken separately, Q changes depending on whether the indices are divided by their number of ingredients, because the two poles contain 12 and 9 ingredients. Throughout the article, "index" refers to P or C, and "prosocial share" refers only to Q. We regressed (Q) on release year. We predicted that the prosocial index would increase while the competitive index decreased, producing an increase in Q.

Because analyses based on annual means may obscure heterogeneity among the games released within each year, we complemented them with three models estimated at the level of the 11,359 individual releases. First, we regressed each index on release year using ordinary least squares to determine whether the trend held at the level of individual games and to quantify the variance it explained without the smoothing introduced by annual averaging. Second, we added genre, number of platforms, and log-transformed global sales as covariates, thereby adjusting the year coefficient for temporal changes in the composition of the corpus along these dimensions. Third, we stacked the observations for the two indices and estimated a pole-by-year interaction, with standard errors clustered by title. This interaction provides a direct estimate of the difference between the temporal trends of the prosocial and competitive poles.

For descriptive purposes, we also regressed the share of each of the 48 ingredients separately on release year, applying the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. These analyses identify which motivations contributed to the overall change, but the primary weight rests on the two composite indices rather than on any individual ingredient. We then assessed the scope and robustness of the result using a series of alternative specifications, detailed in the Robustness section. We tested whether the temporal reallocation held within genres, within single-player and multiplayer titles, within franchises, and among best-selling games. We also examined sales-weighted estimates, changes across the full distribution of games, robustness to removing each ingredient in turn, and every admissible alternative definition of the two indices. Finally, we assessed whether the ingredients' co-occurrence structure changed over time. All analyses used a fixed random seed and can be fully reproduced from the annotated corpus.

2.2 Results

2.2.1 A directional reallocation across the 48 ingredients

When examined separately as a function of release year, the 48 ingredient shares showed a structured, directional pattern of change rather than uniform drift. After Benjamini-Hochberg correction, 29 shares increased significantly, 14 decreased significantly, and 5 showed no reliable temporal trend. The largest increases concerned affiliative and caring motivations: Friendship (+1.04 points of relative share per decade), Warmth (+0.92), Compassion (+0.68) and Affiliation (+0.66), all q < .001. The largest declines concerned skill-focused, strategic and agonistic motivations: Skill acquisition (-1.69), Pride (-1.36), Anger (-1.12), Fear of aggressors (-1.01), Mental time travel (-0.89) and Status-seeking (-0.79), all q < .001 (Figure 1, panel A). Not every increasing ingredient was prosocial or moral. Romantic affiliation (+0.50) and Desire (+0.44), for example, also gained relative share, both q < .001. We therefore interpret the overall pattern as a reallocation away from a predominantly skill-focused and agonistic profile towards more affiliative and caring content. Because several non-prosocial ingredients also increased, however, our central inference rests on the specific contrast between the prosocial and competitive indices rather than on a general moralization of games.

2.2.2 The convergence of the two indices

The two functional indices quantify the reallocation. At the level of individual games, the two poles were strongly opposed (r = -.68, 95% CI [-.69, -.67], N = 11,359; Figure 1, panel B). In the primary year-level regressions, the prosocial index increased by an estimated 5.44 percentage points per decade, or 0.45 points per ingredient (R-squared = .91, p < .001), whereas the competitive index decreased by 6.34 points per decade, or 0.70 points per ingredient (R-squared = .90, p < .001). Averaged over the first three years of the corpus (1993-1995, N = 379), the competitive index accounted for 38.60% of the average game's total motivational content, compared with 12.65% for the prosocial index, a gap of about 26.0 percentage points. Over the final three years (2014-2016, N = 864), the competitive index had fallen to 27.36%, and the prosocial index had risen to 22.98%, narrowing the gap to about 4.4 percentage points. On the per-ingredient scale, the same quantities were 4.29% and 1.05% at the start of the period, and 3.04% and 1.92% at its end (Figure 1, panel C). Read at the endpoints of the observation window, the fitted values placed the prosocial index at 11.03% in 1993 and 23.55% in 2016, and the competitive index at 40.53% and 25.94%, reducing the fitted gap from 29.5 to 2.4 percentage points. Games therefore moved from a marked predominance of competitive over prosocial content towards a substantially reduced gap between the two poles. They did not reverse order within the observed period, however: even in 2016, the average competitive index remained slightly larger than the prosocial index.

Using the game-level data, we tested this convergence directly in a single model by stacking the two poles and regressing index value on release year, pole, and their interaction, with standard errors clustered by title. The pole-by-year interaction was +1.31 percentage points per decade (95% CI [1.24, 1.38], p < .001), indicating that the temporal slope of the prosocial index was about 1.3 points more positive than that of the competitive index. This interaction is one of the quantities for which the two scales do not coincide: on the summed scale the same model returned +13.26 points per decade (95% CI [12.56, 13.97], p < .001). It provides the formal test of the convergence shown in Figure 1, panel C.

2.2.3 The trend holds at the level of individual games

The temporal pattern also held at the level of individual game releases. In unadjusted models estimated across all 11,359 releases, the prosocial index increased by 6.0 percentage points per decade (0.50 per ingredient) and the competitive index decreased by 7.3 percentage points per decade (0.81 per ingredient). These slopes were slightly larger in magnitude than the year-level estimates, but the game-level observations showed substantially greater variability: release year explained approximately 8% (prosocial) and 10% (competitive) of the variance at the game level, compared with approximately 90% in the corresponding year-level models. The high year-level R-squared therefore reflects the smoothing produced by annual aggregation rather than a stronger relationship at the level of individual games. Consistent with this interpretation, a variance decomposition indicated that only about 9% of the variance in the prosocial index and 11% in the competitive index occurred between release years, the remainder occurring between games released within the same year. Adjusting for genre, number of platforms, and log-transformed global sales attenuated but did not eliminate the temporal associations. The adjusted prosocial index increased by 3.9 percentage points per decade (0.32 per ingredient; R-squared = .42, p < .001), whereas the competitive index decreased by 4.5 percentage points per decade (0.49 per ingredient; R-squared = .52, p < .001). Finally, adding a quadratic term for release year provided no evidence of a departure from linearity for either pole (prosocial, p = .21; competitive, p = .45). Thus, within the period examined, we found no evidence that the reallocation was driven by a recent acceleration.

2.2.4 Annotation validation

As described in the Methods, one author, blind to the model's scores, hand-coded 99 games released between 1994 and 2016 on all 21 ingredients used to construct the two indices. The sample was drawn at random within each release year, with the number of entries selected from each year proportional to the number of titles released in that year. This procedure yielded 100 entries. Two entries represented the same game, Backyard NBA Basketball, listed separately for two platforms. We therefore coded the game only once, yielding a final sample of 99 distinct games. This audit served two distinct purposes: first, to establish whether annotation accuracy was sufficient to prevent random error from obscuring a genuine trend (false-negative risk); and second, to estimate how much of the observed trend could be attributable to annotation error systematically correlated with release year (false-positive risk). The thresholds for sufficient accuracy and tolerable systematic bias are design-specific and depend on the observed effect size and sample size (Dubourg & Thouzeau, 2026).

The present design is a game-level OLS with release year as the sole predictor, a standardized beta of .31 for the prosocial share, and N = 11,359 releases. For this design, the minimum true annotation quality required to retain 80% power was rho* = .09 (i.e., the lowest correlation between LLM annotations and the true construct at which the effect would still be detected with 80% power). With 99 paired human-model annotations in the audit, this requirement corresponded to an observed correlation of rho = .25. The required annotation quality decreases as corpus size increases: for an effect of the same magnitude, rho would be .65 at N = 200, .41 at N = 500, .29 at N = 1,000 and .13 at N = 5,000. Thus, the large size of our corpus makes the design highly tolerant of random annotation noise.

Observed agreement exceeded the audit threshold by a wide margin. Human and model annotations correlated at rho = .82 for the prosocial index, .76 for the competitive index, and .87 for the prosocial share. Pooling the 99-by-21 ingredient scores yielded rho = .73. This value partly reflects differences in mean score across ingredients (e.g. games generally scored low on Envy and high on Pride), but after centring scores within each ingredient, the pooled within-ingredient, between-game correlation remained r = .65. Across the 21 individual ingredients, median agreement was rho = .65, and only four correlations fell below .50: Forgiveness (.36), Pride (.43), Shame (.48), Affiliation (.49). Dropping these four ingredients left the estimated temporal increase in the prosocial share within the audit sample virtually unchanged and closely matched across annotation methods (human-coded, +13.8 points per decade, p = .001; model-coded, +13.4, p = .004). The observed trend therefore does not depend on the ingredients with the weakest human-model agreement.

To test for systematic temporal bias, we regressed the model-minus-human discrepancy on release year separately for each index. The estimated drift was +0.09 percentage points per decade for the prosocial index (95% CI [-0.14, +0.31], p = .44), -0.05 for the competitive index ([-0.27, +0.18], p = .69), and +1.15 for the prosocial share ([-2.6, +4.9], p = .55). None was distinguishable from zero. At N = 11,359, a very small bias (gamma = .018 standardized units, or 0.69 points of prosocial share per decade) would be sufficient to produce a significant slope under a true null, compared with the observed slope of 11.59 points per decade. Detecting a bias this small with 80% power would take approximately 5,600 hand-coded games, and the present 99-game audit had a power of only .065 against it. What the audit can rule out is a much larger bias accounting for approximately half or more of the reported effect: its minimum detectable drift was 5.4 points per decade, with simulations yielding a comparable threshold of approximately 46% of the observed effect. Thus, the audit excludes large systematic discrepancies but cannot rule out the small temporal bias that could achieve statistical significance in the full corpus. No realistically sized hand-coding audit could provide that degree of resolution. We therefore conducted further tests that do not depend on the audit's ability to detect such a small bias: subsampling the model-annotated corpus commensurate with the audit's detection limit, testing whether the temporal reallocation could be recovered from the human annotations alone and correcting the corpus-level estimate for annotation error.

The audit constrains the year-correlated component of annotation error. However, the magnitude of bias capable of affecting inference at N = 11,359 is too small to be detected reliably from 99 hand-coded games. A complementary strategy operates on the other term of the same inequality (Dubourg & Thouzeau, 2026): reducing the size of the analyzed corpus rather than increasing the size of the audit. The minimum bias required to produce a significant temporal slope under a true null is not fixed. As the corpus shrinks, the standard error of the year coefficient increases, and a larger undetected bias is therefore needed to produce a false-positive result. In the full corpus, this critical bias is only 0.69 points of prosocial share per decade, which is below the audit's detection limit. At N = 194, however, it rises to 5.42 points per decade, exceeding the upper bound of the audit's 95% confidence interval for the observed drift (4.94). Thus, at N = 194, any year-correlated bias still compatible with the audit is too small, by itself, to produce a significant temporal trend under a true null.

The subsampling strategy has a lower as well as an upper bound, because shrinking the corpus also increases the annotation quality required to avoid a false negative. Given the agreement observed across the 99 audit pairs (rho = .87), the design continued to satisfy this requirement at N = 130 but not at N = 100, where an agreement of rho = .93 would have been required. Combined with the false-positive ceiling derived above, this defined an admissible range of 130 to 194 games. We used N = 193, near the upper end. We then re-estimated the regression of prosocial share on release year in 2,000 random subsamples of 193 releases drawn from the full corpus. The median slope was +11.61 percentage points per decade, with a central 95% empirical interval of [6.58, 16.45], closely matching the full-corpus estimate of +11.59. The slope was positive in all 2,000 subsamples and statistically significant at p < .05 in 99.5% of them.

Results were similar at the lower bound of the admissible range, N = 130: the median slope was +11.63 points per decade, with a central 95% empirical interval of [6.39, 17.15], and 98.7% of subsamples produced a significant slope. Subsampling does not itself reduce annotation bias: each subsample inherits any systematic bias present in the model's annotation. What changes is the magnitude of bias required to produce a significant result under a true null. At sample sizes between 130 and 194, that critical magnitude exceeds the upper bound on year-correlated bias permitted by the audit. The persistence of the trend within this range therefore cannot be explained solely by a systematic drift that the validation failed to detect.

Regressing annotation discrepancies on release year provides an indirect test of systematic model bias. A more direct test removes the model annotations from the loop and asks whether the same temporal reallocation is present in the human-coded data. The bias of concern is one that would make a true null association appear significant. The human annotations provide direct evidence against that null. Across the 99 audited games, the human-coded share increased by 11.9 percentage points per decade (95% CI [+4.8, +18.9], p = .001), compared with 13.0 points for the model annotations of the same games (p < .001). Thus, a coder who was blind to all model outputs recovered the temporal reallocation independently, with an estimated slope closely matching that produced by the model.

The separate indices showed a less symmetrical pattern in this smaller sample. The prosocial index increased under both annotation methods (human-coded: +0.57 scale points per decade, p = .001; model-coded: +0.66, p < .001), whereas the competitive index showed no reliable temporal change under either method (human-coded: +0.01, p = .96; model-coded, -0.04, p = .81). The 99-game audit lacked sufficient power to detect the competitive decline on the raw 0-6 scale; in this subset, the overall reallocation was therefore recovered through the prosocial share measure rather than through a separately significant decline in the competitive index. This limitation is a property of the validation subsample, not of the full corpus, in which the competitive decline is itself significant at N = 11,359.

We conducted two additional checks. First, the model's overall scoring differences favored the competitive rather than the prosocial pole. Relative to the human coder, the model assigned lower scores to prosocial ingredients (mean model-minus-human error = -0.22 on the 0-6 scale) and higher scores to competitive ingredients (+0.29). Thus, the model portrayed games as less prosocial and more competitive overall than did the human coder. These overall scoring differences cannot by themselves explain the observed temporal shift toward the prosocial pole; they could do so only if they varied systematically with release year. Second, we tested for precisely such temporal variation. When the audit sample was split in 2005, pooled human-model agreement was virtually identical in the earlier and later periods (rho = .725 vs .724), and the mean signed difference remained close to zero in both (-0.04 vs +0.02). We therefore found no indication that the estimated reallocation resulted from an era-dependent decline in agreement or a systematic temporal drift in model scores.

Finally, the audit can be used not only to test for bias but to correct for it. Prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023) takes the slope estimated on the full corpus and subtracts the model's drift measured in the audit (i.e., how much faster the model's scores rise over time than the human scores). The confidence interval is widened accordingly, to reflect the uncertainty of this drift. Because the audited games were drawn at random from the corpus, the corrected estimate is valid whether or not the model is biased, even if the bias is too small for the audit to detect. The corrected slope of the prosocial share was +10.44 percentage points per decade (95% CI [+6.64, +14.24], p < .001), close to the uncorrected +11.59, and its interval was about 1.8 times narrower than with human annotations alone. The temporal reallocation toward prosocial content therefore holds once annotation error is corrected.

2.3 Robustness

All robustness analyses address the same central claim: over the period examined, games reallocated their motivational content away from competitive and towards prosocial ingredients. Rather than treating each analysis as a separate finding, we used them to test whether this reallocation persisted under a series of plausible alternative explanations. Specifically, we examined whether the pattern could be attributed to changes in genre composition, the balance between single-player and multiplayer titles, the franchises represented in the corpus, differential commercial success, a small subset of unusually prosocial games, the particular ingredients assigned to the two indices, or changes in how motivations combine (i.e. the ingredients' co-occurrence structure). The reallocation remained evident across all these tests (Table 1).
