The per-ingredient values reported alongside them in the Results follow by division by 12 (prosocial) and 9 (competitive).

2.3.1 Within genres

The temporal reallocation occurred within genre rather than resulting from changes in the genre composition of the corpus. When we re-estimated the two index trends separately within each of the 12 genres, the prosocial index increased significantly in 11 of the 12 genres and the competitive index decreased significantly in 10. The prosocial increase was nonsignificant only for Strategy games, whereas the competitive decrease was nonsignificant only for Strategy and Role-Playing games. In a pooled model with genre fixed effects, in which the year coefficient was identified only from temporal variation within genres, the prosocial index increased by 3.7 percentage points per decade (0.31 per ingredient) and the competitive index decreased by 4.2 points per decade (0.46 per ingredient), both p < .001. Because each slope is estimated within a single genre, the pattern cannot be attributed to changes in the relative prevalence of genres characterized by more prosocial or more competitive content (Figure 2).

2.3.2 Single-and multiplayer titles

The temporal reallocation was evident in both single-and multiplayer games. For each platform version of a game, GPT-5.5 indicated whether local multiplayer (several players on a single device) and online multiplayer (several networked devices) were available at release (yes, no, or not determinable). A title's local-and online-multiplayer shares are the proportions of its platform versions offering each feature. We classified a title as multiplayer when either its localor online-multiplayer share was at least .50 and re-estimated the two index trends separately within each mode. Among single-player titles, the prosocial index increased by 4.5 points per decade (0.37 per ingredient) and the competitive index decreased by 4.8 points (0.54 per ingredient); among multiplayer titles, the corresponding changes were +5.2 and -6.1 points per decade (+0.44 and -0.68 per ingredient), all p < .001. The year-by-mode interaction indicated that the reallocation was, if anything, slightly steeper among multiplayer titles (prosocial, +1.5 points per decade, p < .001; competitive, -1.2 points, p < .001). Because the same pattern appeared in games involving human co-players, it cannot be explained solely by the increasing use of algorithmically simulated companionship in single-player games (Figure 3).

We further divided multiplayer titles according to whether their multiplayer content was predominantly local (n = 4,028) or online (n = 2,170), and compared them with single-player titles (n = 5,161). The same reallocation appeared in all three categories. In single-player, local-multiplayer, and online-multiplayer titles, respectively, the prosocial index increased by 4.5, 4.3, and 5.5 percentage points per decade, whereas the competitive index decreased by 4.8, 5.5 and 3.9 (all p ≤ .001).

Relative to single-player titles, the prosocial increase did not differ among online-multiplayer titles (+0.65 points per decade, p = .26), and the competitive decline was weaker (+2.63 points per decade, p < .001). The reallocation was therefore not concentrated in the titles most exposed to online play, which argues against reducing it to the spread of online connectivity.

2.3.3 Within franchises

The temporal reallocation documented thus far compares games released in different years, leaving open a compositional explanation: successive waves of releases may draw on different franchises, such that the aggregate trend reflects which franchises entered or disappeared from the market rather than changes within the franchises themselves. To address this possibility, we examined whether successive installments of the same franchise shifted towards the prosocial pole.

To identify franchises, we provided the full list of titles in the annotated corpus to a large language model (Claude Opus 4.8) and instructed it to group releases belonging to the same franchise. This procedure identified 832 franchises covering 6,063 releases. The automatic grouping procedure sometimes merged unrelated titles that shared short, generic name prefixes. We therefore first audited the groups most at risk, flagging those whose assigned franchise name either consisted of a single common English word or formed a prefix of another franchise name. These criteria identified 121 candidate groups, which we inspected manually. Fifty-nine proved to combine unrelated titles on the basis of a shared word. For example, the group labeled "Space" included Space Jam, Space Hulk, and Space Chimps. We removed these groups, leaving 773 franchises comprising 5,673 releases. To estimate the residual error rate after this audit, we manually inspected a random sample of 30 retained franchises. Twenty-eight formed coherent series and two did not, corresponding to an estimated residual error rate of 6.7%. Because erroneous groups combine unrelated titles, they should add noise and attenuate the within-franchise estimates towards zero rather than generate a systematic temporal trend, provided that grouping errors are not themselves associated with release year.

For each index, we regressed its value on release year with franchise fixed effects and standard errors clustered by franchise. The year coefficients were therefore identified exclusively from temporal variation within franchises. Later releases within a franchise were, on average, more prosocial and less competitive than earlier releases: the prosocial index increased by 2.5 percentage points per decade (0.21 per ingredient), whereas the competitive index decreased by 2.2 points (0.25 per ingredient), both p < .001. These within-franchise slopes were about half the magnitude of the corpus-wide slopes, consistent with stable differences between franchises contributing to the aggregate pattern. Nevertheless, both retained the predicted direction and remained highly significant. Estimated franchise by franchise among the 576 franchises spanning at least four distinct release years, the prosocial index rose in 65.8% and the competitive index fell in 62.7%, with both moving in the predicted direction in 48.6%. FIFA illustrates how this reallocation can occur without removing competition from the game. Across its 37 titles, the prosocial share (Q) rose from 11.4% to 21.8%, while the raw scores of key competitive motivations remained stable: Pride was rated 5 in every edition, and Anger and Coalitional affiliation were rated as high in the latest editions as in the 1990s (4 and 5.9 on the 0-6 scale).

The model describes team rivalry as "one of the game's clearest motivational structures" in both FIFA 17 and FIFA: Road to World Cup 98. The motivational repertoire surrounding match play expanded, with the summed score across all ingredients rising from 56 to 74. Resource accumulation showed the largest increase, from 0.1 to 3.5: the model describes early titles as "not built around stockpiling money, materials, or consumables", whereas later editions introduce career-mode budgets and transfers and, eventually, Ultimate Team, where players earn coins, collect cards and build squads. Competition thus remained central to match play but came to occupy a smaller share of a broader motivational repertoire. Holding franchise identity constant, later installments therefore devoted a larger proportion of their motivational content to prosocial ingredients and a smaller share to competitive ingredients (Figure 4).

2.3.4 Best-selling titles and sales weighting

The temporal reallocation was also present among the games with the greatest commercial reach, although its magnitude depended on the weight assigned to the largest sellers. Restricting each release year to its best-selling titles left the prosocial increase significant at every threshold tested, from the top 10 to the top 100 titles per year. Among the annual top 100, the prosocial index increased by 4.4 percentage points per decade (0.37 per ingredient, p < .001). The competitive decrease was significant at every threshold from the top 30 onwards but not in the more restrictive top 10 sample, where the slope was indistinguishable from zero (-0.004 points per decade, p = .99) and each year contributed only 10 observations.

We also weighted each game in proportion to its global sales, thereby giving greater influence to titles that sold more copies. Sales weighting attenuated both temporal slopes but preserved their direction and statistical significance: the prosocial index increased by 4.0 percentage points per decade (0.33 per ingredient) and the competitive index decreased by 2.5 points (0.27 per ingredient), compared with unweighted estimates of +6.0 and -7.3 points (+0.50 and -0.81 per ingredient), respectively. This attenuation suggests that lower-selling titles contributed disproportionately to the magnitude of the unweighted reallocation. Nevertheless, the shift remained significant both among the best-selling titles and when all releases were weighted by their commercial reach (Figure 5, panel B).

2.3.5 Across the distribution of games

The reallocation was not confined to a fringe of unusually prosocial games but was evident across the distribution of releases. Quantile regressions of each index on release year yielded positive prosocial slopes at the 10th (+3.6 percentage points per decade, 0.30 per ingredient), 50th (+7.9, 0.66), and 90th (+3.8, 0.32) percentiles (all p < .001), with the largest estimated increase occurring at the median. The competitive index declined at all three percentiles as well (-6.0, -8.3, and -6.5 points per decade; -0.67, -0.93, and -0.72 per ingredient; all p < .001), again most steeply at the median. If the aggregate had been driven solely by an increasingly prosocial upper tail, little or no change would have been expected at the median or lower quantiles. Instead, all three quantiles increased substantially. The reallocation therefore characterized the typical game released in each year, rather than only a small group of outlying titles.

2.3.6 Independence from any single ingredient

Neither temporal trend depended on any single constituent ingredient. We recomputed each index after excluding its ingredients one at a time, yielding 12 leave-one-out specifications for the prosocial index and 9 for the competitive index. In every specification, the temporal slope retained its original direction and remained significant. Excluding Friendship produced the largest attenuation of the prosocial trend, yet the prosocial index still increased by 4.4 percentage points per decade (0.40 per ingredient); excluding Pride produced the largest attenuation of the competitive trend, which still declined by 5.0 points (0.62 per ingredient) (Figure 5, panel A). A bootstrap over games with 1,000 resamples likewise yielded narrow intervals around both year-level slopes: +5.4 per decade for the prosocial index (95% bootstrap interval [5.0, 5.9]) and -6.3 for the competitive index (95% bootstrap interval [-6.8, -5.9]). The two trends therefore reflect changes distributed across the ingredients composing each pole rather than changes in any single motivation.

2.3.7 Robustness to alternative index definitions

The temporal reallocation was robust to the particular composition of the two indices. We conducted a multiverse analysis (Steegen et al., 2016), recomputing the prosocial share Q = P/(P+C) for every admissible pair of ingredient subsets containing at least 6 of the original 12 prosocial ingredients and at least 5 of the original 9 competitive ingredients, each subset divided by its own size so that specifications of different sizes remain comparable. The procedure yielded 642,560 alternative index definitions. Regressing Q on release year across the 11,359 releases, Q increased significantly in every specification (range +6.4 to +17.0 percentage points per decade; median +11.6, against +11.6 for the reference definition) (Figure 5, panel C). Thus, within this admissible specification space, no choice of which ingredients count as prosocial or competitive removed or reversed the effect.

2.3.8 Stability of the ingredient co-occurrence structure

Finally, we examined whether the temporal reallocation was accompanied by a broader change in how motivational ingredients combine within games. We constructed separate 48-by-48 ingredient co-occurrence matrices for the early (1993-2004, n = 3,925) and later (2005-2016, n = 7,434) halves of the period. The two matrices showed a very strong correspondence (Mantel r = .93, p < .001, 9,999 permutations), indicating that the overall pattern of which motivations tended to occur together remained highly stable. The reallocation therefore primarily concerned the relative prevalence of different motivations within a stable co-occurrence structure, rather than a reorganization of that structure. This result does not imply that every pairwise relationship remained unchanged, but it provides no evidence of a large-scale transformation in the motivational architecture of games.

Taken together, Study 1 shows that, between 1993 and 2016, the motivational content of games shifted away from competition and dominance and towards affiliation, warmth, and care. The temporal slope of the prosocial index was approximately 1.3 points per decade more positive, on the per-ingredient scale, than that of the competitive index, substantially narrowing the initial gap in favor of the competitive pole. This shift reflected a compositional reallocation of motivational content rather than a general increase in motivational richness over time. The reallocation was evident at the level of individual game releases, survived adjustment for genre, number of platforms, and global sales, and extended across the distribution of games. It also held within genres, play modes, and franchises, among best-selling and sales-weighted titles, after removing each ingredient in turn, and across every admissible alternative index definition. The prosocial increase held in every one of these specifications; the competitive decline, while robust overall, was attenuated among the highest-selling titles. Finally, the trend was independently recovered from the human annotations, while the broader co-occurrence structure of motivational ingredients remained highly stable.

3. Study 2: Personality predicts players' preferred motivational content

Study 1 established that the balance of motivational content in games shifted over two decades, away from the agonistic pole of status, anger, hatred, revenge and towards the caring pole of affiliation, friendship, warmth and compassion. One implication of a medium that tracks its audience's motivations is that attraction to these forms of content should vary systematically across individuals. Study 2 therefore examines whether players' Big Five personality traits predict the relative balance of prosocial and competitive motivations in their favorite games.

The design also distinguishes two forms of sociality that are often conflated. One concerns the social context of play: a preference for playing with -and often competing against -other people.

The other concerns the social content of play: a preference for games that engage motivations related to care, warmth, and affiliation. These are distinct preferences, which we expected to load on personality traits: preference for a social play context with Extraversion, reflecting sociability and assertiveness, and preference for prosocial content with Agreeableness, reflecting warmth and concern for others.

3.1. Method

Player data were collected through a gamified online platform launched in 2024. After completing the assessment (a personality inventory and a short questionnaire on gaming habits, approximately 15 minutes), users received a personalized player profile and game recommendations. The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Université Paris Cité (IRB No. 00012024-50) on June 11, 2024, and was conducted in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). All participants provided informed consent. For each participant, we recorded their preferred game genres, up to five favorite games entered as free text, total number of games played, weekly playing time, age, and gender. Personality was assessed using the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2-S), which yields scores for five broad personality domains and 15 facets, with three facets nested within each domain (Soto & John, 2017).

The initial sample comprised 4,657 players. Gender was self-reported from four options: 3,785 reported male, 713 female, 67 non-binary or third gender, and 92 preferred not to report it. Because the latter two groups were too small to yield stable estimates, we restricted analyses to the 4,498 players who reported male or female (mean age = 32.6 years; 15.9% women). Gender was modeled as a binary variable. Our estimates therefore describe the contrast between men and women, and their applicability to the 159 excluded players remains untested. Every listed game was annotated on the same 48 motivational ingredients as in Study 1, using the same large-language-model procedure (GPT-5.4, identical prompt). Annotation was run separately, on the game names as written by participants. Because some names were ambiguous (e.g., "fifa"), titles present in both corpora did not receive identical scores, but these correlated at r = .86. After excluding game entries for which motivational content could not be coded, the dataset contained 21,539 player-game observations.

For each game, we calculated the prosocial (P) and competitive (C) index scores using the same fixed lists of 12 and 9 ingredients, respectively, as in Study 1, each divided by its number of constituent ingredients. We then expressed the game's position within this two-pole composition as the prosocial share, Q = P / (P+C), with the complementary competitive share given by 1-Q = C / (P+C) Thus, Q represents the proportion of the game's caring-plus-agonistic content allocated to the caring pole (M = .39, SD = .12).

Because the two shares are exact complements, linear models predicting them are mirror images: each predictor has coefficients of equal magnitude but opposite sign. We therefore report only the model predicting the prosocial share. Positive coefficients indicate a preference for more caring relative to agonistic content, whereas negative coefficients indicate the reverse.

3.2. Analyses

Players completed the BFI-2-S, from which we calculated scores for the five broad personality traits (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness) and their 15 constituent facets. All trait and facet scores were standardized before analysis; the outcome Q was left on its original scale.

We fitted a linear mixed-effects model predicting the prosocial share Q of each listed game from the five traits, so that coefficients express the change in Q associated with a one-standard-deviation difference in a trait. The model included a random intercept for players to account for the clustering of multiple games within players, together with age, gender, weekly playing time, and years of gaming experience as covariates. Because all five domains were included in the same model, each coefficient represents the association with one trait adjusted for the other four. Fixed effects were tested using Wald z tests. Because Q is a property of the game rather than of the player, every nomination of the same title carries the same value. We nonetheless checked that the trait-level results held under standard errors clustered by both player and title.

We then conducted three complementary analyses using the same covariate and random-effects structure. First, to determine whether Agreeableness predicted specifically the relative composition of motivational content rather than overall motivational richness, we fitted a parallel model with the summed raw score across all 48 ingredients as the outcome. Second, we fitted a facet-level model in which the five domain scores were replaced by the 15 BFI-2-S facet scores. Third, we constructed an ingredient-level personality fingerprint by fitting 48 separate models, each with one of the raw ingredient scores as the outcome and the five domain scores entered simultaneously as predictors. The resulting 240 p-values (48 outcomes * 5 traits) were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

3.3. Results

Personality traits were systematically associated with the relative balance between the two motivational poles. All coefficients reported below come from the model predicting the prosocial share (Q). Positive coefficients therefore indicate a shift towards the caring pole, whereas negative coefficients indicate a shift towards the agonistic pole.

Extraversion predicted a lower share (b = -0.006, z = -5.36, p < .001), whereas Agreeableness predicted a higher share (b = 0.003, z = 3.47, p < .001). Conscientiousness (b = 0.005, z = 4.48, p < .001 ) was also associated with a greater relative preference for the caring pole, as were Neuroticism (b = 0.003, z = 2.56, p = .011 ), and, more weakly, Openness (b = 0.002, z = 2.02, p = .043). These associations were modest but statistically reliable: a one-standard-deviation difference in a trait corresponded to a shift of between 0.2 and 0.6 percentage points in Q . Gender showed a substantially larger association. Holding the other predictors constant, women's listed games had a prosocial share (Q) approximately 4.7 percentage points higher than men's (b = 0.047, z = 17.0, p < .001), an effect more than eight times larger than the largest personality-trait coefficient (Figure 6). Under standard errors clustered by both player and title, the associations with Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness and Neuroticism, and that of gender, remained significant, whereas the association with Openness did not (p = .065). The associations between personality traits and the prosocial share were largely consistent across genders. Estimated separately, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness were significant predictors among men (N = 3,785 players), and Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness (p = .049) and Neuroticism among women (N = 713); Openness reached significance in neither group. None of the five trait-by-gender interactions was significant (all p ≥ .08), providing no evidence that these associations differed by gender. The association with Agreeableness concerned the relative composition of motivational content rather than its overall richness. Agreeableness predicted a higher prosocial share (b = 0.003, p < .001) but was unrelated to the summed intensity of the 48 motivational ingredients (b = -0.022, p = .92). Thus, the favorite games of more agreeable players were not motivationally richer overall; instead, a greater proportion of their motivational content was allocated to the caring rather than the agonistic pole. This pattern argues against the alternative explanation that agreeable players simply prefer games with denser or more motivational content.

The facet-level results sharpened, and partly complicated, the trait-level pattern. Positive associations with the prosocial share (Q) emerged for Aesthetic sensitivity (a facet of Openness, b = 0.005) and Compassion (a facet of Agreeableness, b = 0.004). By contrast, the strongest negative association was observed for Sociability, the facet of Extraversion most directly related to social engagement (b = -0.003), followed by Trust, a facet of Agreeableness (b = -0.003, p = .011). These four associations survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the 15 facets; Anxiety (b = 0.003) and Respectfulness (b = 0.002) do not.

That Sociability predicted a preference for relatively more agonistic rather than caring content is consistent with the distinction between social context and social content. A disposition towards seeking social interaction does not necessarily imply a preference for games whose content centers on care, warmth and affiliation. These two forms of social preference appear to relate to different aspects of personality. The 48-ingredient profile of Agreeableness provided a more nuanced account than the simple conclusion that more agreeable players prefer caring content.

Its largest raw-score associations were negative and concerned agonistic ingredients: higher Agreeableness was associated with lower scores for Status-seeking (b = -0.061), Coalitional affiliation (-0.050), Envy (-0.044), Revenge (-0.033), Fear of aggressors (-0.031), Shame (-0.030) and Anger (-0.027). Among the caring ingredients, Warmth was the only one showing a significant positive association (b = 0.026). Affiliation was instead negatively associated with Agreeableness (b = -0.032), whereas Compassion, Friendship, and Familial love showed no reliable associations. The same contrast appeared in the ingredient-level profile of Extraversion, which mirrored that of Agreeableness: positive associations for Status-seeking (b = 0.078), Coalitional affiliation (0.052), Shame (0.047), Fear of aggressors (0.045), Envy (0.042) and Anger (0.039), and negative ones for Warmth, Compassion, Friendship and Familial love. All ingredient-level models entered the five domains simultaneously and were Benjamini-Hochberg corrected across the 240 tests.

The positive association between Agreeableness and the prosocial share therefore did not reflect a broad preference for caring motivations. It arose substantially from lower scores on agonistic ingredients: because Q=P/(P+C), a reduction in competitive content necessarily increases the relative prosocial share even if prosocial content does not increase. Together with the specific positive association with Warmth, this pattern suggests that the Agreeableness effect reflects a relative avoidance of agonistic content more than a general attraction to care.

4. General Discussion

Across two studies, we document a historical reallocation in the motivational content of video games and show that preferences along the same dimension covary with individual differences in personality. In Study 1, the prosocial index, the share of games' motivational content devoted to prosocial motivations -including affiliation, friendship, warmth, and compassion -increased between 1993 and 2016, whereas the competitive index devoted to agonistic motivationsincluding status, anger and revenge -decreased. The temporal slope of the prosocial index was approximately 1.3 points per decade more positive, on the per-ingredient scale, than that of the competitive index, substantially narrowing the initial gap between the two poles. Because the analysis captured relative composition rather than absolute motivational intensity, this pattern reflects a reallocation of motivational content rather than merely the general increase in motivational richness over time. We refer to this historical shift as a "prosocial turn."

Study 2 complements this historical analysis by asking whether the same motivational axis also explains variation in players' preferences. Players higher in Agreeableness listed favorite games with a larger prosocial share -an association driven primarily by lower agonistic contentwhereas players higher in Extraversion showed the reverse pattern. Together, the two studies connect a historical trend with a corresponding dimension of individual variation: the shift occurred in the direction of the preferences associated with higher Agreeableness and lower Extraversion. This correspondence does not, however, establish that historical changes in the composition of the gaming audience caused the shift.

We interpret this convergence between the historical shift and contemporary player preferences through the entertainment technology hypothesis (Dubourg & Baumard, 2022). This framework represents entertainment products as bundles of motivational ingredients that engage evolved preferences, with each ingredient defined by the fundamental motive it activates (Dubourg, Thouzeau, et al., 2026). A game's appeal should therefore depend partly on the match between its motivational composition and the preferences of its audience, while popular culture may more broadly reflect the preferences to which it caters (Saad, 2011). From a cultural-evolutionary perspective, the distribution of content within a medium should change when the environment created by audience preferences changes. New cultural variants are continually generated, and those that fit available cognitive niches are more likely to be adopted and retained. Through repeated cycles of production, selection, and transmission, a cultural repertoire may therefore shift towards cultural attractors grounded in consumers' minds (Claidière & Sperber, 2007; Claidière et al., 2014; Acerbi & Mesoudi, 2015; Mesoudi, 2016). The prosocial turn can be interpreted as the cultural signature of a changing alignment between the motivational content offered by games and the preferences of their audience.

At least three non-exclusive mechanisms could have produced this realignment, and our data cannot distinguish between them. The first possibility is an "audience-composition" account (Figure 7, panel A): as gaming expanded beyond its early audience, the distribution of player preferences may also have shifted.

If the groups entering the market were, on average, less attracted to status and conflict and more attracted to care and affiliation, the changing composition of the player population could have altered demand for these different forms of motivational content. This possibility is consistent with the substantial gender difference observed in Study 2 and with previous evidence of gendered game preferences (Lucas & Sherry, 2004; Lange et al., 2021). Nevertheless, the personality associations were similar in direction among men and women, with no significant trait-by-gender interactions. This suggests that dispositional differences in preferences along the caring-agonistic axis were present in both groups. Long-running ESA and ISFE reports also document an increasing representation of women and older players since the late 1990s. These demographic series are external to our corpus, however, and cannot establish that changes in audience composition caused the historical shift in game content.

A second possibility operates at a broader level than the first. Under a "psychological-ecological" account (Figure 7, panel B), the shift need not reflect changes specific to the composition of the gaming audience. Instead, the wider population may have shifted, on average, towards greater cooperation, tolerance, and concern for others. This account treats such dispositions as responsive to local ecological conditions. When access to basic resources such as food, health care, and education is secure, individuals are hypothesized to adopt slower, more future-oriented life strategies, which in turn favor patience, trust, and concern for others (Dubourg et al., 2026; Baumard et al., 2015; Baumard & Chevallier, 2015; Sheskin et al., 2014). Because the decades our corpus spans were, in most of the markets it covers, decades of rising affluence, this account predicts a broader shift towards prosocial and caring dispositions, accompanied by a corresponding change in the values expressed in cultural products (Baumard & André, 2025). Related mechanisms have been invoked to explain the historical rise of prosociality in Western fiction (Martins & Baumard, 2020) and the postmaterialist shift in values documented by decades of survey research (Inglehart et al., 2017). On this interpretation, the prosocial turn in video games may be another cultural trace of the same long-term realignment, with games serving as a relatively recent medium in which it can be observed. Of the three accounts, this one connects our findings most directly to the broader literature on how material security may reshape human motivation (Boon-Falleur et al., 2025).

A third possibility is a "design-drift" account (Figure 7, panel C), under which neither the composition nor the preferences of the player population need have changed. Instead, new technological and design affordances (including persistent worlds, cooperative mechanics, parasocial relationships with characters, and online connectivity) may have expanded developers' capacity to represent and sustain caring forms of motivational content. Study 1 speaks against the strongest version of this account, in which the prosocial turn results primarily from the emergence of online or multiplayer gaming. The reallocation was also present in single-player titles and within long-running franchises. Although it was slightly steeper among multiplayer titles considered as a single group, the prosocial increase did not differ reliably across single-player, local multiplayer and online multiplayer titles when the three categories were compared. It therefore cannot be reduced to the arrival of multiplayer or internet connectivity. A broader design-drift account nevertheless remains plausible, because many relevant affordances also transformed single-player games. Distinguishing changes in who plays from changes in what designers can build would require longitudinal data linking audience composition and preferences to evolving design capabilities and game content. We regard this as a central question for future research.

The present work has several limitations. First, the corpus is restricted to console and PC titles tracked through unit sales and excludes mobile and free-to-play games, which constitute a substantial segment of contemporary gaming. Our estimates should therefore be interpreted as characterizing the traditional console and PC market rather than video games as a whole.

Although the accessibility and social orientation of many mobile and free-to-play games suggest that their inclusion might strengthen the observed trend, this possibility remains to be tested. Second, Study 2 is cross-sectional. It establishes that personality traits covary with preferences for motivational content among players, but it cannot show that the trait composition of the gaming audience changed over the period examined in Study 1. Longitudinal evidence of such a change would be required to test the audience-composition account directly. Finally, the personality associations were modest, consistent with those typically observed between broad traits and specific behaviors (Vize et al., 2023; Mammadov, 2022; Entringer et al., 2021), while gender showed a substantially larger association with motivational-content preference. We therefore interpret the personality findings as evidence that stable dispositions are associated with players' content preferences, not as evidence that changes in those dispositions drove the historical shift.

Figure 7.

Figure 7. Three non-exclusive accounts of the prosocial turn. Each account could produce the observed increase in the prosocial share (Q) of game content (bottom), and the present data cannot distinguish between them. Circles represent the player population before and after the shift; grey boxes summarise the mechanism at work in each panel. (a) Audience-composition: new players with different preferences enter the market, altering demand for motivational content, while existing players' preferences remain unchanged. The larger circle reflects the expansion of the player population. (b) Psychological-ecological: existing players become more prosocial as part of a broader shift in the population (e.g., because of rising material security). The values expressed in cultural products shift accordingly. (c) Design-drift: the player population is assumed to be predominantly prosocial and remains unchanged in composition and preferences. New technological and design affordances, such as cooperative mechanics and bonds with characters, expand developers' capacity to represent and sustain caring content. This allows game content to catch up with players' existing preferences.
